title: Getting started
source: apps/docs/content/docs/getting-started.md
url: https://greatcms.dev/docs/getting-started
---

# Getting started

> Scaffold a site's configuration, connect it to the studio, publish.

## Set up a repository

```sh
npx greatcms init
```

It detects what you build with — Astro, Next, Nuxt, SvelteKit, or Eleventy — and
puts content where that generator already looks for it. Eleventy gets
`_data/cms`, Astro gets `src/content/cms`, Next gets `content/cms`. It prints the
small reader integration for that framework, so schema defaults render before a
content file has ever been written.

You end up with two commented files: `.cms/schema.yaml` describing what may be
edited, and `.cms/config.yaml` describing where it goes.

For a product or service business, start with the recurring pieces already
wired together:

```sh
npx greatcms init --template business
```

That gives editors company, owner/contact and search details, a hero,
reorderable page sections for features, ordered processes, statistics, stories,
products, FAQs and calls to action, and JSON collections for products and pages.
The CMS supplies the content shape; your own components still decide how every
section looks.

Render the pages collection through one dynamic route in your framework. An
editor can then add an About, Services, or legal page as a normal collection
entry; `showInNavigation` and `navigationOrder` make the menu update from the
same data. See `examples/business-astro/src/pages/[slug].astro` for the complete
Astro version.

## Add another kind of section

Define it and make it selectable in the page editor with one command:

```sh
npx greatcms add section testimonial --to home.sections \
  --field quote:richtext! --field name:text!
```

If the schema has only one reorderable region, `--to` is optional. Implement
the new `_type: "testimonial"` case once in your site's section renderer; from
then on editors can add, remove and reorder testimonials without touching YAML
or adding another route.

## Read a region

A region resolves to plain data. In Astro, read it through the schema-aware
reader so a brand-new region renders its defaults before its JSON file exists:

```js
import { createReader } from "@greatcms/reader";
const cms = createReader();
const hero = cms.region("home.hero");
```

In Eleventy, with no import at all, because `_data` is global data:

```njk
<h1>{{ cms["home.hero"].heading }}</h1>
```

The same reader infers types when you run `greatcms types`.

## Connect it

Run the studio and add the site. Point it at **a folder on this machine** and it
reads and writes that working copy directly — no token, no network. Give it your
dev server's URL and the editor shows your real components beside the form.

The studio reads your schema and builds the editor from it. It never runs any
code from your repository.

## Check it

```sh
npx greatcms doctor
```

Prints every region, the file it resolves to, and which are still rendering
schema defaults.

To check the content itself — in a build, or before you push:

```sh
npx greatcms check
```

It validates every content file and collection entry against your schema, and
exits non-zero if anything would not render: a required field left empty, a
field the schema no longer has, a file no region renders, an image pointing at
something nobody committed. `--json` reports the same to a machine.

A region with no content file is not a failure — it renders schema defaults,
which is the point.


---
title: The command line
source: apps/docs/content/docs/the-command-line.md
url: https://greatcms.dev/docs/the-command-line
---

# The command line

> Scaffold, extend, type, check, and inspect a site from the terminal.

Everything the CLI does runs on your machine with your toolchain. It edits the
two files in `.cms/`, reads your content, and never talks to the studio.

## `greatcms init`

```sh
npx greatcms init
```

Detects the framework (Astro, Next, Nuxt, SvelteKit, Eleventy, or nothing in
particular), puts content where that generator already looks for it, writes a
commented `.cms/schema.yaml` and `.cms/config.yaml` with the editor's `$schema`
line for autocomplete, and prints the snippet that reads your first region in
your framework's own syntax.

Templates: `hero` (one region), `landing` (a page of reorderable blocks),
`business` (a complete small-business content model), `blog`, and `blank`.
`--yes` takes every default, and `--framework`, `--template`, `--name`, and
`--dir` override one answer each, so it scripts as well as it prompts. It
refuses to overwrite an existing setup without `--force`.

## `greatcms setup`

```sh
npx greatcms setup ./my-project
```

The guided version. It scans the target directory, detects the framework and
package manager, and finds child projects as well as apps under `apps/`,
`packages/`, and `examples/`. Choose a discovered app or the folder itself, then
either start from a template or build a content model field by field: regions,
reusable sections, reorderable page sections, collections, and groups for
related details such as an owner or opening hours.

Every planned file is shown before anything is written, and cancelling writes
nothing. The scan reads configuration data only. It does not execute project
code, follow symbolic links, or look inside dependencies.

## `greatcms add`

The second managed section is the one that used to mean hand-editing YAML.

```sh
npx greatcms add region about.intro --field heading:text! --field body:richtext
npx greatcms add section testimonial --to home.sections --field quote:richtext! --field name:text!
npx greatcms add block card --field title:text! --field body:text
npx greatcms add collection guides --format mdx --field content:richtext
```

A field is `name:type`, with a trailing `!` for required. Types are `text`,
`richtext`, `image`, `link`, `number`, `boolean`, `date`, `file`, `select(a|b)`,
`list(text)`, and `blocks(card|grid)` for a nested list. `add section` defines a
block and adds it to a reorderable region's allow list in one edit; when the
schema has only one such region, `--to` is optional.

The schema is edited **as text**, so the comments explaining your site's own
decisions survive. It refuses rather than corrupts: a duplicate name, an id the
standard would reject, or a nested block that does not exist all stop before
the file changes. Run it with no fields in a terminal and it asks.

## `greatcms types`

```sh
npx greatcms types --out src/cms.d.ts
```

An interface for every region, block, and collection, with select options as
unions and blocks discriminated by `_type`, plus a module augmentation that
types the reader by id. `cms.region("home.heroo")` becomes a compile error. A
field with a `default` is non-optional, because resolution guarantees it a
value.

`--check` exits non-zero when the committed file no longer matches the schema,
which is how CI notices a schema change nobody regenerated the types for. A
site that never runs it loses nothing: without the file, the reader takes any
string.

## `greatcms check`

```sh
npx greatcms check
# content: OK (3 regions, 6 entries, 1 media reference)
```

Validates every content file and collection entry against the schema and exits
non-zero if anything would not render: a required field left empty, a field
the schema no longer has, a file no region renders any more, frontmatter that
will not parse, an image pointing at a file nobody committed. Each report names
the file, the field path, and what to do. `--json` gives the same report to a
machine.

A region with no content file is never a failure. It renders schema defaults,
and `check` says so.

## `greatcms doctor`

Prints every region, the file it resolves to, which ones are still rendering
schema defaults, and any unsaved edit left in `.cms/draft/`: the one thing that
shows in your dev server and nowhere else.


---
title: The hybrid model
source: apps/docs/content/docs/the-hybrid-model.md
url: https://greatcms.dev/docs/the-hybrid-model
---

# The hybrid model

> Why a region is opt-in, and what happens before anyone edits anything.

Most of a page is code. A headline, a pricing table, and a rotating set of
feature cards are not — those change on a marketing schedule rather than a
release schedule, and they are the reason people install a CMS at all.

GreatCMS manages only what you list. Everything else is ordinary code the studio
never sees, never parses, and cannot break.

## Regions

A **region** is a named slice of a page: `home.hero`, `pricing.faq`. The id
doubles as the file name, so `home.hero` is stored at
`<regions dir>/home.hero.json`.

A **blocks region** holds an ordered list an editor can add to and reorder, from
a set of block types you allow. A **collection** is a folder of entries sharing
a shape — a blog, case studies, a changelog — stored as Markdown with
frontmatter, which is what every static site generator already expects.

## Defaults are not a fallback, they are the starting state

A missing content file is never an error. The region resolves to the `default`
values declared in the schema, so a site is correct **before the CMS has ever
run**, and stays correct if a field is added to the schema before anyone edits
it.

Stored content layers over those defaults: objects merge deeply, arrays are
replaced wholesale, and each block in a list is merged over its block type's
own defaults.

## What a site depends on

Its own files. There is no network call, no database, and no API key in a build.
The schema is part of the site and is committed alongside the code. What a site
never depends on is the studio: shut it down permanently and every site it
managed keeps building.


---
title: Publishing
source: apps/docs/content/docs/publishing.md
url: https://greatcms.dev/docs/publishing
---

# Publishing

> One commit in your working copy, or nothing at all.

A site is a folder on the machine the studio runs on. Publishing writes the
content files into that folder and commits them on whatever branch is checked
out. The commit is the deploy trigger: push it, and whatever CI the repository
already had does the rest. There is no webhook to configure and no cache to
purge.

A folder that is not a Git repository works too. The files are written, and
that is the whole job.

## One commit, or none

A publish touching a region and three uploaded images is **one commit**. Every
file is written to a temporary file first and then moved into place, so a full
disk or a bad path fails before any real file has changed. If Git refuses the
commit (a held `index.lock`, a missing `user.email`, a path in `.gitignore`), the
editor says so instead of reporting a publish that never happened.

Publishes to the same folder run one at a time, so a double-click or two open
tabs cannot interleave their writes.

The studio never runs your repository's Git hooks. They are code in the
repository, and the studio does not execute anything from a repository it
manages. Checks belong in CI, where they run on every commit anyway.

## Pushing for you

For an editor who should never see Git, turn on **Push after every publish**
in the site's settings. Each publish is then pushed to the branch's upstream,
and the host deploys it the way it deploys any push: edit, publish, live.

The push uses the Git credentials of the machine the studio runs on, never
prompts for a password, and never runs a pre-push hook. If it fails, the
commit is still there and the editor is told it is not live yet, with the
reason: most often the remote has commits this copy lacks, which
`git pull --rebase` in the site's folder sorts out. Publishes waiting to go
out are listed on the site's page, with a **Push now** button.

## Conflicts

A publish carries the commit the editor started from. If the content being
published changed since then, in a newer commit or as an uncommitted edit
someone made by hand, the publish is refused rather than overwriting it. Reload,
then publish again. A commit that touched other files is not a conflict, so
working on the site's code does not interrupt anyone editing its content.

Creating an entry never replaces one: if the title would produce a file name
that already exists, the studio asks for a different one.

## Validation happens first

Content is checked against the schema before anything is written, so invalid
content never reaches the repository. Alt text is part of that: the only way to
store an empty one is a field explicitly marked `alt: decorative-allowed`.

Run `greatcms check` in CI to hold hand-edited content to the same rules.


---
title: Running the studio
source: apps/docs/content/docs/running-the-studio.md
url: https://greatcms.dev/docs/running-the-studio
---

# Running the studio

> One process, one SQLite file, one password. Nothing it manages depends on it.

The studio is a single Node process. It keeps its own state, the list of sites
and the submissions inbox, in one SQLite file, and reads and writes the sites it
manages as folders on the same machine.

```sh
STUDIO_PASSWORD='something long' pnpm --filter @greatcms/studio start
# GreatCMS studio on http://localhost:8787
```

Or as a container: `apps/studio/Dockerfile` builds one image with one volume
for the database. `STUDIO_PASSWORD` is required and deliberately has no default.
For a server that also builds and serves the site, see
[Self-hosting](/docs/self-hosting/).

## Environment

| Variable               | Meaning                                                                                                     |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `STUDIO_PASSWORD`      | Required. Changing it signs every open session out.                                                         |
| `STUDIO_SECRET`        | Signs session cookies. Generated on start if unset, which means sessions reset on restart.                  |
| `STUDIO_DB`            | Path to the SQLite file. Defaults to `data/studio.sqlite`.                                                  |
| `PORT`                 | Defaults to `8787`.                                                                                         |
| `STUDIO_SITES`         | Sites to manage from the first start, as JSON; see [Self-hosting](/docs/self-hosting/).                     |
| `STUDIO_URL`           | Where browsers reach the studio, so a proxy's `forward_auth` can send visitors here to sign in.             |
| `STUDIO_COOKIE_DOMAIN` | Parent domain the sign-in is shared across, e.g. for `preview.`; see [Self-hosting](/docs/self-hosting/).   |
| `STUDIO_TRUST_PROXY`   | `1` behind a reverse proxy you control, `cloudflare` behind Cloudflare. Unset when reachable directly.      |
| `RESEND_API_KEY`       | With `NOTIFY_FROM` and `NOTIFY_TO`, emails each form submission. Without them, submissions are only stored. |

Behind a proxy, `STUDIO_TRUST_PROXY` lets rate limiting see the visitor's
address rather than the proxy's, and marks the session cookie `Secure`. The
studio uses the last `X-Forwarded-For` entry, the one your proxy appended, or
`CF-Connecting-IP` for Cloudflare. Leave it unset when the studio is reachable
directly: those headers are then the visitor's to forge.

## Connecting a site

A site is a folder on the machine the studio runs on. Add it by path, and the
studio reads `.cms/schema.yaml` from that working copy and builds the editor
from it. There is no token and no network call. Give it your dev server's URL
and the editor frames your real site beside the form; see
[Previewing](/docs/previewing/).

## What it will not do

The studio never executes anything from a repository it manages: not a build,
not a Git hook, not a schema that happens to be code. Schemas are data. A
preview is your own dev server. Checks belong in CI, where they run on every
commit anyway.

Shut the studio down and every site it managed keeps building from what is in
Git. That is the point of the whole arrangement, and it is why one studio can
manage several sites without carrying a toolchain for each.

## Security headers and rate limits

Every response carries a strict `Content-Security-Policy`, and a preview URL
the browser would execute (`javascript:`, `data:`) is refused. Sign-in attempts
and form intake are rate limited per address, and uploads are checked by their
bytes rather than their extension: an SVG, which can carry script, is refused as
an image.


---
title: Self-hosting
source: apps/docs/content/docs/self-hosting.md
url: https://greatcms.dev/docs/self-hosting
---

# Self-hosting

> One server, three containers; an editor publishes and the site is live in seconds.

Nothing here needs a platform. A site built with GreatCMS is files, so the whole
of it, editing included, fits on one small server:

- **The studio**, where editors sign in and publish. Each publish is a commit in
  the site's working copy on that server.
- **The builder**, `greatcms-deploy`, which watches that working copy, builds
  every new commit in a clean checkout, and swaps the live folder when the build
  succeeds. A failed build changes nothing; the previous release stays up.
- **A web server** serving the live folder, with the studio behind the same
  reverse proxy. Caddy gets HTTPS for free.

Editors never touch Git, a terminal, or a dashboard. Publish, wait a few
seconds, reload.

## The builder

```sh
DEPLOY_SOURCE=/srv/sites/my-site DEPLOY_ROOT=/srv/www npx greatcms-deploy
```

It checks the branch tip every few seconds. For a commit that is not live it
clones the repository into a work folder, runs the build command (by default
`pnpm install --frozen-lockfile && pnpm build`), moves the output into
`releases/<sha>`, and repoints the `current` symlink in one rename. Serve
`DEPLOY_ROOT/current` and a visitor always sees a whole release, never a
half-written one. The last few releases are kept so you can roll back by moving
the symlink.

| Variable          | Meaning                                                         |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `DEPLOY_SOURCE`   | The repository: a path on the server, or any URL git can clone. |
| `DEPLOY_ROOT`     | Holds `releases/`, `current` and `status.json`.                 |
| `DEPLOY_BUILD`    | The build command. Runs in the checkout with `CI=1`.            |
| `DEPLOY_OUTPUT`   | The folder the build writes, relative to the checkout. `dist`.  |
| `DEPLOY_BRANCH`   | `main`.                                                         |
| `DEPLOY_INTERVAL` | Seconds between checks. `10`.                                   |
| `DEPLOY_KEEP`     | Releases kept for rollback. `5`.                                |

`status.json` records what is live and, until a later commit builds, the newest
one that failed with the tail of its build log. `greatcms-deploy status` prints
it; `greatcms-deploy once` builds and exits, for a cron job or a CI step.

The builder is the only part of the arrangement that runs the site's own code,
and it does so in a container of its own with nothing but a clone in it. The
studio still executes nothing from a repository it manages; see
[Running the studio](/docs/running-the-studio/).

## Declaring sites up front

A server should come up already managing its sites, under ids that do not
change between restarts, because the id is part of the form address every
contact form posts to. `STUDIO_SITES` does that:

```sh
STUDIO_SITES='[{"id":"my-site","path":"/srv/sites/my-site","devUrl":"https://preview.example.com","pushAfterPublish":false}]'
```

On start the studio adds any site it does not have and brings the rest in line
with the list. An id that already points at a different folder is refused
rather than silently moved.

## Live preview on the server

The editor frames the site's dev server beside the form, so a change is seen
rendered before it is published. On a server that means running the dev server
there too, in the same working copy the studio writes drafts into, and it must
not be open to the world.

The studio vouches for it. `GET /auth/check` answers `204` when the request
carries a signed-in session and otherwise redirects to the studio's sign-in,
which comes back to the page that was wanted. Caddy's `forward_auth` asks it
before every preview request:

```
preview.example.com {
	forward_auth studio:8787 {
		uri /auth/check
	}
	reverse_proxy preview:4321
}
```

For the preview to see the same sign-in, the session cookie is set for the
parent domain, and the studio has to know its own address for the redirect:

| Variable               | Meaning                                                        |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `STUDIO_URL`           | Where browsers reach the studio, `https://studio.example.com`. |
| `STUDIO_COOKIE_DOMAIN` | The parent domain, `example.com`. Unset: this host only.       |

A redirect is only ever issued to a host under that domain. With both set, an
editor who is signed in to the studio sees the preview, in the frame and in a
tab, and nobody else does. There is no second password. The dev server itself
has to accept the name it is reached by; the example passes `PREVIEW_HOST` to
Astro's `vite.server.allowedHosts`.

The preview is optional: without it the editor still publishes, and the
builder shows the result a few seconds later.

### Only while someone is editing

A dev server is the one heavy process in the stack, and it is only useful
while an editor is looking. `greatcms-preview`, in the same package and image
as the builder, stands where the dev server would: the first request starts
it, every request keeps it alive, and after `PREVIEW_IDLE` seconds of silence
(fifteen minutes by default) it is stopped. While it comes up the browser gets
a small page that asks again every two seconds, so the editor's frame fills in
by itself.

| Variable          | Meaning                                                               |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `PREVIEW_SOURCE`  | The site's working copy, the same folder the studio writes drafts to. |
| `PREVIEW_COMMAND` | Starts the dev server on `$PORT`; default installs and runs Astro.    |
| `PREVIEW_IDLE`    | Seconds without a request before it is stopped.                       |

`GET /__greatcms/preview` reports whether it is stopped, starting or running.
Reloads reach the dev server over the same proxy, WebSockets included, so a
draft still shows as you type. The example stack runs it this way, and a
site that nobody edits all day costs a few megabytes of the proxy and nothing
else.

## A complete example

`examples/business-astro/deploy/` holds a `compose.yaml` and `Caddyfile` that
run all of this on one machine from one setting. `DOMAIN=example.com` in
`.env` gives the site at the apex and `www`, the studio at `studio.example.com`
and the preview at `preview.example.com`, with Caddy on 80 and 443 fetching
certificates for all four. Clone the site into `/srv/sites`, point the four
DNS records at the server, and `COMPOSE_BAKE=false docker compose up -d --build`
(the images build on the host network, which the bake builder refuses). The same files
with `compose.local.yaml` run everything on `localhost` ports first; browsers
share cookies across ports, so the sign-in covers the preview there too.


---
title: Previewing
source: apps/docs/content/docs/previewing.md
url: https://greatcms.dev/docs/previewing
---

# Previewing

> Your own dev server renders it. Never the studio.

## In your own dev server

Point a local site at your dev server's URL and the editor shows your real
components beside the form. Publishing writes the files, your dev server
reloads, and the pane updates — usually within a couple of seconds.

For a Vite-based site this needs one plugin:

```js
import { greatcmsWatch } from "@greatcms/reader/vite";
export default defineConfig({ vite: { plugins: [greatcmsWatch()] } });
```

The reader reads content with the filesystem, which is what keeps it
framework-neutral, and it also means Vite has no idea those files are
dependencies. Without the watcher the file changes and the page does not.

## As you type, in your own site

Connect a site as a folder on this machine, give it your dev server's URL, and
the editor shows that dev server beside the form. Each edit is written to
`.cms/draft/` in your working copy; your dev server notices and reloads, so your
own components render content nobody has published.

There is no approximation of your design, because there is no approximation: it
is your site. Publishing writes the real content file and clears the draft.

Three rules keep drafts safe. The reader only reads them when `NODE_ENV` is
`development`, so a build can never render one. `.cms/draft/` ignores itself, so
one can never be committed. And publishing clears the draft it came from, so the
site stops showing an edit that has already landed.

Without JavaScript nothing is written as you type, and the editor still
publishes — the frame simply shows the site as last published.

## Pointing at the page

The framed page knows what the form holds. Switch on **Select** above the
preview and the page is dissected: move over it and the heading, paragraph,
image or section under the pointer is outlined with its field's name; click,
and that field opens and takes focus in the form. **Sections** outlines every
block on the page at once, so a long page reads as the list of sections it is.
It runs the other way too: land in a field in the form and the page scrolls to
where it renders. The header and footer belong to site regions rather than to
the page, and they are on the page all the same: click the footer while editing
a page and the Footer editor opens at the field you clicked.

No markup is needed for this. The inspector matches each field's value to what
the page shows, which covers headings, copy, rich text and images. Where a site
transforms a value before printing it, or shows the same words twice, two
attributes make the match explicit:

```html
<h2 data-greatcms-field="blocks.0.title">{title}</h2>
<section data-greatcms-block="block-0">…</section>
```

The field path is the one the form uses, dotted; a block's id is `block-` and
its position. Both are plain attributes, so a built page keeps them and nothing
reads them there.

The inspector is part of the script the dev server injects while the page is
framed, so a visitor never downloads it and the studio never reaches into your
page: the two sides talk only through messages, each checking the other is
who framed it.

## Opening the page being edited

By default the frame opens the front of the site. Tell the studio where each
collection's entries live and it opens the page you are editing instead:

```yaml
# .cms/config.yaml
preview:
  paths:
    pages: { home: "/", "*": "/{slug}" }
    updates: "/updates/{slug}"
```

A plain path with `{slug}` covers most collections; a map lets one slug be the
front page. Regions, which are part of every page, preview at `/`.

## Getting rid of an unsaved edit

Leave the editor and come back and the draft is still in the form, with a
notice saying so: the preview and the form always show the same thing, and
publishing publishes what you see. "Discard unsaved edits" beside the frame
throws the draft away and puts your dev server back to what is published. It
is a plain form post, so it works with JavaScript switched off.

Anything still unsaved is listed on the site's page in the studio, and
`npx greatcms doctor` names it from the terminal — a draft you forgot is
otherwise visible only in dev, which is exactly where you would stop noticing
it.

If your dev server is not Vite-based, the watcher plugin cannot reload it for
you; **Reload the site** beside the frame does it by hand.

## Pages built from a collection

Astro's dev server caches what `getStaticPaths()` returns. If it passes each
entry to the page as a prop, the preview keeps showing that cached copy and
never your edit. Return only the slug, and read the entry in the page itself:

```astro
---
export function getStaticPaths() {
  return cms.collection("pages").map((page) => ({ params: { slug: page.slug } }));
}

const page = cms.collection("pages").find((entry) => entry.slug === Astro.params.slug);
---
```

A build reads each entry once either way, so this costs nothing in production.

## The studio never builds your site

The studio cannot render a Hugo site, or a Laravel one, so it does not pretend
to. Building your site inside the studio would also break the rule that it never
executes anything from a repository it manages. Your dev server renders the
preview, on your machine, with your toolchain; your CI builds what you publish.


---
title: Forms and submissions
source: apps/docs/content/docs/forms-and-submissions.md
url: https://greatcms.dev/docs/forms-and-submissions
---

# Forms and submissions

> The one thing Git cannot hold, collected in one inbox.

Git cannot hold a message someone typed on your site. The studio takes it
directly, so there is no third-party form service and no per-site backend to
provision.

```html
<form method="POST" action="https://your-studio/f/{siteId}/contact">
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required />

  <input type="hidden" name="_redirect" value="/thanks/" />
  <input type="hidden" name="_t" value="1755024000000" />

  <button>Send</button>
</form>
```

No JavaScript is involved. Adding a site to the inbox is a row in a table.

## Reserved fields

| Field       | Meaning                                                     |
| ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `_redirect` | Where to send the visitor afterwards. Same-site paths only. |
| `_t`        | When the form was rendered, in epoch milliseconds.          |
| `company`   | Honeypot. Hide it visually _and_ from assistive technology. |

## Spam

Scored from the honeypot, the gap between render and submit, and link density —
never a CAPTCHA, which taxes every legitimate visitor to inconvenience a bot
that solves them anyway. Suspected spam is stored and hidden rather than
discarded, so nothing is lost silently.

## Limits

Each visitor address may submit 20 times a minute. Each site stores at most
1,000 submissions a day and sends at most 60 notification emails an
hour, however many addresses the traffic comes from. Past the email limit,
submissions are still stored; they just stop arriving in your mailbox until the
hour turns over.

Submissions across every site land in one inbox, with read state, CSV export,
and optional email notification.


---
title: Accessibility
source: apps/docs/content/docs/accessibility.md
url: https://greatcms.dev/docs/accessibility
---

# Accessibility

> What is enforced by the format, and what is enforced by tests.

Accessibility here is structural where it can be, and a test where it cannot.

## Enforced by the format

`alt` is required on every image field by default. A field may declare
`alt: decorative-allowed`, which is the only way an empty alt validates — making
an inaccessible image a deliberate authoring act rather than an oversight.
Invalid content is refused before it reaches your repository.

Image width and height are read from the uploaded file's own header and stored
alongside it, so pages do not reflow while images load.

## Enforced by tests

The studio ships **zero JavaScript**. Every screen is server-rendered and every
mutation is a form POST — including adding, removing, and reordering blocks in a
block list. That is what makes the editor keyboard-operable and
screen-reader-legible by construction, rather than by patching ARIA onto
hand-built widgets.

axe runs against every studio screen and every page of the example site on each
CI run, with zero violations allowed. Errors are attached with `aria-invalid`
and `aria-describedby` rather than colour alone. The example site carries a
weight budget so "fast" cannot quietly stop being true.


---
title: Any language
source: apps/docs/content/docs/any-language.md
url: https://greatcms.dev/docs/any-language
---

# Any language

> The standard is files. A reader in Python passes the same suite as the one in TypeScript.

A site is managed by GreatCMS if it contains a schema file and reads content
from the paths the standard describes. That is the entire integration surface.
Hugo, Jekyll, Laravel, or a hand-rolled Go generator consume it exactly as
Astro does, because none of them need anything but YAML and JSON.

The JavaScript packages are a convenience, not a requirement.

## What a reader has to get right

Four cases, all of them in the conformance fixtures because naive
implementations get them wrong:

- **A region with no content file.** It resolves to the schema's `default`
  values. It is not an error.
- **Content written before a field was added.** The new field takes its default;
  the stored fields are kept.
- **A block missing a defaulted field.** Each block in a list is merged over its
  own block type's defaults.
- **A decorative image with empty alt text.** Valid only when the field is
  marked `alt: decorative-allowed`.

The rules are in [section 6 of the standard](/spec/#6-resolution-rules-the-important-part):
objects merge deeply, arrays are replaced wholesale, and a missing schema is a
loud error where a missing content file is not.

## Proving it

```sh
npx @greatcms/conformance fixtures        # prints the path to the fixture site
python3 read.py "$(npx @greatcms/conformance fixtures)" ./out
npx @greatcms/conformance verify ./out
# conformance: PASS
```

Point your reader at the fixture site, write every resolved region to
`<region-id>.json`, and, if it implements collections,
`entries/<collection>/<slug>.json`. The verifier compares each against the
expected document and reports collections separately, so a regions-only reader
still gets a useful answer.

## The reference in Python

`examples/reader-python/read.py` is a complete reader in about 120 lines of
Python, standard library plus PyYAML, written from the standard alone. CI runs
it against the fixtures on every build. It exists to keep the project honest:
if integrating in a new language needs more than one file's worth of code, the
standard has drifted towards whatever is convenient for JavaScript, and that is
a bug.

One detail it has to handle: the standard reads YAML 1.2, where `no` and `off`
are strings and a date is a string. PyYAML implements 1.1, so the reader
replaces the implicit type resolvers rather than patching the results.

## The machine-readable surface

The schemas for both `.cms` files are published as JSON Schema, which is what
gives editors autocomplete and lets a tool in any language validate a schema
before reading content:

- [/json-schema/schema.schema.json](/json-schema/schema.schema.json)
- [/json-schema/config.schema.json](/json-schema/config.schema.json)

For agents, [/llms.txt](/llms.txt) indexes every page, [/llms-full.txt](/llms-full.txt)
holds them in one fetch, and [/docs.json](/docs.json) lists the integration
steps. Every page here is also served as Markdown at its own path plus `.md`.


---
title: For coding agents
source: apps/docs/content/docs/for-agents.md
url: https://greatcms.dev/docs/for-agents
---

# For coding agents

> Every surface an agent needs to wire a site up unattended, and the skill that teaches it.

"Integrate from the standard in half an hour" should hold for a coding agent as
much as for a person. These are the surfaces, each reachable in one fetch, each
generated from the same sources as the pages people read, so they cannot
drift.

| Surface                              | Address                                    |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------ |
| Index and integration summary        | `/llms.txt`                                |
| Every document in one file           | `/llms-full.txt`                           |
| Each page as Markdown                | `/spec.md`, `/docs/<page>.md`, `/index.md` |
| Manifest with entry points and steps | `/docs.json`                               |
| JSON Schema for `.cms/schema.yaml`   | `/json-schema/schema.schema.json`          |
| JSON Schema for `.cms/config.yaml`   | `/json-schema/config.schema.json`          |

## The skill

The repository ships an agent skill, `skills/greatcms/SKILL.md`: the commands,
the file shapes, the pitfalls and the checks, written to be followed without a
person in the loop. Install it into Claude Code, Cursor or any agent that
reads the open skills format:

```sh
npx skills add greatcms/greatcms@greatcms
```

## In the repository

`greatcms init` leaves a section in the site's `AGENTS.md` between
`<!-- greatcms:start -->` and `<!-- greatcms:end -->`, saying where content
lives, what to run before committing, and what not to touch. Running `init`
again updates that section and leaves the rest of the file alone.

Two commands produce machine-readable output for an agent to act on:

```sh
npx greatcms check --json     # every content file against the schema; exit code for CI
npx greatcms doctor --json    # regions, collections, what is still at defaults, unsaved drafts
```

Errors from every command carry their remedy on a `fix:` line, in the exact
text that reaches stderr, so an agent can apply it rather than guess.

## What an agent should never do

Call the studio from a page, write into `.cms/draft/`, or ship JavaScript from
GreatCMS to a public site. The [invariants](/docs/the-hybrid-model/) are the
same for agents as for people.


---
title: The examples
source: apps/docs/content/docs/examples.md
url: https://greatcms.dev/docs/examples
---

# The examples

> Two Astro sites and a Python reader, each built to prove one thing.

Every example in the repository is also a test. They build in CI, run axe with
zero violations allowed, and assert that their output contains no script tag.

## A minimal site

```sh
pnpm --filter @greatcms/example-site-astro dev     # http://localhost:4321
```

`examples/site-astro` is the smallest honest demonstration. The home page puts a
managed hero next to a hand-written section, and both end up in the same static
HTML. A managed block list holds features and pull quotes an editor can
reorder. A blog collection is Markdown with frontmatter, which is what every
static site generator already expects. A contact form posts straight to the
studio with no JavaScript.

The about page is the interesting one: there is no `about.intro.json` in the
repository, so it renders the defaults declared in the schema. The page was
correct before the studio had ever been opened.

## A complete small business

```sh
pnpm --filter @greatcms/example-business-astro dev
```

`examples/business-astro` is what `greatcms init --template business` grows
into: a fictional seed cooperative with company, contact, and search details;
a home page of reorderable sections (feature grids, an ordered process,
statistics, a story with an image, a product showcase, FAQs, a call to action);
a JSON collection of products, each with its own page; and a collection of
managed pages rendered through one dynamic route.

That last part is the point. Adding an About or a privacy policy is one new
collection entry: the page, its menu item, and its footer link appear together,
and the schema is untouched. The components are site-owned, so the CMS supplies
content shapes and never a look. Its tests build the site with real images in
place and check that width, height, and alt text all survive to the HTML.

## This site

`apps/docs` is the website you are reading. The landing page's headline, the
claims, and the closing note are JSON in the repository, edited in the studio.
The layout around them is ordinary Astro. The standard page renders `SPEC.md`
directly, so the published document and the one the code implements cannot
drift, and the docs pages are a Markdown collection like any blog.

## A reader in Python

`examples/reader-python/read.py` reads the standard without any of the
JavaScript packages and passes the conformance suite. See
[Any language](/docs/any-language/).

## Running any of them from the studio

Start the studio, add the example's folder as a site, and give it the dev
server's URL. Edits appear in your own dev server as you type, and publishing
commits to this repository like it would to yours.
